response.sql: WITH gender_counts AS (SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM Orders o JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.date_order_placed BETWEEN '2013-10-25 17:40:25' AND '2017-05-24 19:26:44' GROUP BY c.gender), avg_count AS (SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_order_count FROM gender_counts) SELECT g.gender, g.order_count, g.order_count - a.avg_order_count AS above_average FROM gender_counts g CROSS JOIN avg_count a WHERE g.order_count > a.avg_order_count;

assumptions.assumption: The average is the unweighted mean of the per-gender order counts, so each gender group counts once regardless of its size.
Orders are kept only when a matching Customers row exists (inner join). Customers with a NULL gender form their own group, which the GROUP BY includes.
date_order_placed is stored as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' text, so the string BETWEEN bounds compare correctly and include both endpoints.

alternatives.interpretation: Exclude customers whose gender is NULL, so only genders that are actually recorded are compared against the average.
alternatives.sql: WITH gender_counts AS (SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM Orders o JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.date_order_placed BETWEEN '2013-10-25 17:40:25' AND '2017-05-24 19:26:44' AND c.gender IS NOT NULL GROUP BY c.gender), avg_count AS (SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_order_count FROM gender_counts) SELECT g.gender, g.order_count, g.order_count - a.avg_order_count AS above_average FROM gender_counts g CROSS JOIN avg_count a WHERE g.order_count > a.avg_order_count;
